question: What news does Hanani bring from Jerusalem, and how does Nehemiah react in the following days?
What word given to Moses does Nehemiah remind God of, and why does it support the request he makes?
The verb שָׁמַר (shamar, “keep”) appears for God, who keeps the covenant, and for the people, who were to keep the commandments: how does the prayer play on these two faithfulnesses?
Nehemiah says “both I and my father's house have sinned”: what difference does it make to include yourself in the confession when you pray for a group?
What requests does Nehemiah make of the king, one after another, and what happens between the king's question and his answer?
Why does Nehemiah inspect the walls at night and tell no one his plans before seeing the situation?
The verb קוּם (qum, “rise up”) appears in the people's answer and in Nehemiah's answer to the mockers: what attitude does it express in the face of the challenge?
Between the king's question and the answer, Nehemiah “prayed to the God of heaven”: what would it be like to pray this way, in a few seconds, in the middle of a hard conversation?
What kinds of people appear working on the wall (priests, goldsmiths, perfumers, leaders, daughters), and who refuses to work?
Why does the text record so many times that someone made repairs “in front of his house,” and what does this say about the way the work was organized?
The verb translated “repair” is חָזַק (chazaq, “be strong, strengthen”), repeated through almost the whole chapter: what image does this word add to the work on the wall?
The “nobles” of Tekoa refuse to serve, while other Tekoites even repair a second section (3:27): where would your name appear in this list?
How do Sanballat and Tobiah mock the work, and what images do they use to belittle it?
The people pray to God and also post guards day and night: how does the chapter combine trust in God and practical measures?
The word מְלָאכָה (melakhah, “work”) is repeated while the people work armed: what changes in the way the work is done in the face of the threat?
Nehemiah says “remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers”: what do you do when fear threatens to stop something important?
What three kinds of complaint do the people present, and who is behind the oppression?
What contradiction does Nehemiah point out between redeeming brothers sold to the nations and what the nobles were doing?
The verb נָשָׁה (nashah, “lend at interest”) is at the center of the crisis: what did Israel's Law say about loans among brothers, and why does Nehemiah include himself in the fault?
Nehemiah gives up a legitimate right, “the governor's food allotment,” because of the burden on the people: what right could you give up for the sake of others?
How many times do the enemies invite Nehemiah to the plain of Ono, and what changes with the fifth invitation?
Why does Nehemiah refuse Shemaiah's advice to hide in the temple, and how does he perceive that the prophecy was false?
The verb יָרֵא (yare, “fear,” here “intimidate”) appears several times: who tries to cause fear, by what means, and how does the chapter end regarding the enemies' fear (6:16)?
Nehemiah answers “I am doing a great work, so I cannot come down”: what distractions do you need to refuse in order to finish what you began?
What measures does Nehemiah take after the wall is finished, and what problem still exists in the city?
Why does Nehemiah turn to the list of those who returned with Zerubbabel, almost the same as Ezra 2, and what does it mean at this moment of the story?
The verb יָחַשׂ (yachas, “enroll by genealogy”) appears at the beginning and end of the record: why did belonging to the people depend on this record?
Hananiah is chosen for being “a faithful man who feared God more than most”: what qualities do you look for in someone who receives a responsibility?
Where, for how long and before whom does Ezra read the Law, and what do the Levites do during the reading?
Why do the people weep on hearing the Law, and why do the leaders say it is not a day of sorrow?
The verb בִּין (bin, “understand, discern”) is repeated throughout the reading: what does the text show is necessary for the people to understand?
“The joy of the LORD is your strength”: how can this phrase be read at a moment when you feel guilty or weak?
How do the people prepare for the confession, and how much time do they devote to reading and worship?
What pattern is repeated in the story the prayer tells, between the people's unfaithfulness and God's response?
The word רַחֲמִים (rachamim, “compassion, mercies”) returns several times in the prayer: at what moments of Israel's history is it remembered?
The people say “we are slaves today” in their own land: how do you pray when you still live with the consequences of mistakes, yours or others'?
What concrete commitments do the people make in the covenant (marriages, Sabbath, seventh year, offerings)?
What does it mean to commit oneself “with a curse and an oath,” and why do the people put the covenant in writing?
The word מַעֲשֵׂר (maaser, “tithe”) appears even as “a tenth of the tithes”: how did the tithes support the temple service, according to this chapter?
The chapter ends with “we will not neglect the house of our God”: what concrete commitment would give body to this intention in your life?
How is it decided who will live in Jerusalem, and how do the people treat those who volunteer?
Why was it necessary to populate Jerusalem, and why could living there be seen as a sacrifice?
The verb נָדַב (nadav, “volunteer, offer oneself willingly”) describes those who agree to live in Jerusalem: where else does this verb appear in Ezra and Nehemiah, and with what meaning?
Mattaniah is remembered as “the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer”: what quiet role do you play that helps others to praise or to work?
How is the procession organized at the dedication of the walls, and where do the two choirs meet?
Why does the chapter bring together lists of priests and Levites from several generations before describing the celebration?
The word תּוֹדָה (todah, “thanksgiving”) even names the choirs that walk on the wall: what is the point of calling the choirs this at the dedication?
The rejoicing of Jerusalem “was heard far away”: what celebration of your community shows outsiders what God has done?
What did Eliashib do with the room in the house of God, and what does Nehemiah do on his return?
What commitments of chapter 10 appear broken in this chapter, and what does this suggest about the end of the book?
The verb זָכַר (zakhar, “remember”) appears in Nehemiah's short prayers: what does he ask God to remember, about himself and about others?
Nehemiah reacts with physical harshness to the mixed marriages: how do you evaluate these methods, and how do you deal with your own reaction to others' wrongdoing?
